full_proof.text:
Let
\[
(x)_r=x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1),\qquad (x)_0=1,
\]
denote the falling factorial. We use the usual convention for binomial coefficients of nonnegative integers, in particular \(\binom uv=0\) when \(v>u\).

For \(n>5\), the exact inclusion–exclusion formula for the sequence is
\[
a(n)=\left|\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k (n-1-k)!\,B_{n,k}\right|,
\tag{1}
\]
where
\[
B_{n,k}=
\sum_{j=\max(0,k+5-n)}^{\min(k,4)}
 \binom{8-j}{j}\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}.
\tag{2}
\]
(The absolute value in (1) is harmlessly the ordinary absolute value of the integer inclusion–exclusion sum.) For \(n\leq 5\), \(a(n)=0\), but those finitely many values have no effect on an asymptotic assertion.

We shall prove that
\[
a(n)\sim e^{-2}(n-1)!.
\tag{3}
\]
We will then show that the expression proposed in the conjecture is also asymptotic to the same quantity.

First factor \((n-1)!\) out of (1). For \(0\leq k<n\),
\[
(n-1-k)! = \frac{(n-1)!}{(n-1)_k}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a(n)=(n-1)!\left|
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k\frac{B_{n,k}}{(n-1)_k}
\right|.
\tag{4}
\]
Thus the main point is to establish
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k\frac{B_{n,k}}{(n-1)_k}
\longrightarrow e^{-2}.
\tag{5}
\]

We prove (5) by dominated convergence for series. Define, for all nonnegative integers \(n,k\),
\[
f_n(k)=
\begin{cases}
(-1)^k B_{n,k}/(n-1)_k,&k<n,\\
0,&k\geq n,
\end{cases}
\qquad	ext{and}\qquad
g(k)=\frac{(-2)^k}{k!}.
\tag{6}
\]
We will prove, first, that for every fixed \(k\),
\[
f_n(k)\longrightarrow g(k),
\tag{7}
\]
and, second, that for all \(n\geq8\) and every \(k\),
\[
|f_n(k)|\leq \frac{3^k}{k!}.
\tag{8}
\]
Since \(\sum_{k\geq0}3^k/k!=e^3<\infty\), these two facts imply that the sums of the \(f_n(k)\)'s converge to the sum of the \(g(k)\)'s.

We begin with the pointwise limit. Fix \(k\). Once \(n\geq k+5\), the lower endpoint in (2) is zero, so
\[
B_{n,k}=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,4)}
 \binom{8-j}{j}\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}.
\tag{9}
\]
We consider separately the term \(j=0\) and those with \(j>0\).

For \(j=0\), use \(\binom mr=(m)_r/r!\) to write
\[
\frac{\binom{2n-k-10}{k}}{(n-1)_k}
= rac1{k!}\frac{(2n-k-10)_k}{(n-1)_k}.
\tag{10}
\]
For sufficiently large \(n\), the second quotient is
\[
\frac{(2n-k-10)_k}{(n-1)_k}
=
\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}
\frac{2n-(k+10+i)}{n-(1+i)}.
\tag{11}
\]
Every factor on the right tends to \(2\). There are only \(k\) factors, so (11) tends to \(2^k\). Since \(\binom80=1\), the normalized \(j=0\) term therefore tends to
\[
\frac{2^k}{k!}.
\tag{12}
\]

Now let \(1\leq j\leq\min(k,4)\). We show that
\[
\frac{\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}}{(n-1)_k}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{13}
\]
Here is an explicit bound. Put \(r=k-j\). Comparing the factors in the two falling factorials gives
\[
(2n+j-k-10)_r\leq 2^r(n-1-j)_r.
\tag{14}
\]
Indeed, for \(0\leq i<r\),
\[
2n+j-k-10-i\leq 2(n-1-j-i),
\]
with the same inequality still valid under the standard nonnegative-integer subtraction conventions; multiplying these nonnegative factorwise inequalities proves (14). Since
\[
\binom{2n+j-k-10}{r}r!=(2n+j-k-10)_r,
\]
we obtain
\[
\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}(k-j)!
\leq 2^{k-j}(n-1-j)_{k-j}.
\tag{15}
\]
Also, because \(j\geq1\), the initial piece \((n-1)_j\) is at least \(n-j\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Splitting the denominator as
\[
(n-1)_k=(n-1)_j(n-1-j)_{k-j},
\]
and using (15), we get
\[
0\leq
\frac{\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}}{(n-1)_k}
\leq
\frac{2^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}\frac1{n-j}.
\tag{16}
\]
The right side tends to zero. This proves (13). Multiplication by the fixed coefficient \(\binom{8-j}{j}\) does not change the limit. There are only finitely many positive \(j\)'s, so (9), (12), and (13) yield
\[
\frac{B_{n,k}}{(n-1)_k}\longrightarrow\frac{2^k}{k!}.
\tag{17}
\]
For fixed \(k\), eventually \(k<n\); multiplying (17) by \((-1)^k\) gives
\[
f_n(k)\longrightarrow (-1)^k\frac{2^k}{k!}= rac{(-2)^k}{k!},
\]
which is (7).

We next prove the uniform bound (8). The essential estimate is
\[
B_{n,k}\,k!\leq 3^k(n-1)_k
\qquad(n\geq8,\ k<n).
\tag{18}
\]
We prove this term by term in the sum defining \(B_{n,k}\). Every index occurring there satisfies \(j\leq k\) and \(j\leq4\). For \(0\leq j\leq4\), a direct evaluation of these five small cases gives
\[
\binom{8-j}{j}\leq\binom7j.
\tag{19}
\]
Since \(n\geq8\), monotonicity in the upper argument then gives
\[
\binom{8-j}{j}\leq\binom{n-1}{j}.
\tag{20}
\]
We already proved in (15) that
\[
\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}(k-j)!
\leq2^{k-j}(n-1-j)_{k-j}.
\tag{21}
\]
Moreover,
\[
k!=(k-j)!(k)_j.
\tag{22}
\]
Multiplying (20) and (21), and then using (22), shows that the \(j\)-th summand in \(B_{n,k}\), after multiplication by \(k!\), is at most
\[
\binom{n-1}{j}(k)_j\,2^{k-j}(n-1-j)_{k-j}.
\tag{23}
\]
The elementary identity
\[
\binom{n-1}{j}(k)_j(n-1-j)_{k-j}
=\binom{k}{j}(n-1)_k
\tag{24}
\]
follows immediately by writing both binomial coefficients in terms of falling factorials (or by cancelling \(j!\)). Therefore (23) equals
\[
\binom{k}{j}2^{k-j}(n-1)_k.
\tag{25}
\]
All summands are nonnegative. We may consequently enlarge the actual range of \(j\) in (2) to all \(0\leq j\leq k\). Summing (25) and applying the binomial theorem gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_{n,k}k!
&\leq (n-1)_k\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}2^{k-j}\\
&=(n-1)_k(1+2)^k
=3^k(n-1)_k.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (18).

If \(k<n\), both \((n-1)_k\) and \(k!\) are positive, and (18) implies
\[
|f_n(k)|=\frac{B_{n,k}}{(n-1)_k}\leq\frac{3^k}{k!}.
\]
If \(k\geq n\), then \(f_n(k)=0\), so the same inequality is immediate. Thus (8) holds.

The pointwise convergence (7), the summable majorant (8), and dominated convergence for series now imply
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}f_n(k)
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-2)^k}{k!}
=e^{-2}.
\tag{26}
\]
By definition, \(f_n(k)=0\) for \(k\geq n\), so its infinite sum is exactly the finite sum in (5). Hence (5) follows. Since \(e^{-2}>0\), continuity of absolute value gives
\[
\left|\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k\frac{B_{n,k}}{(n-1)_k}\right|
\longrightarrow e^{-2}.
\tag{27}
\]
Combining (27) with (4),
\[
\frac{a(n)}{e^{-2}(n-1)!}
=
\frac{
\left|\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^kB_{n,k}/(n-1)_k\right|
}{e^{-2}}
\longrightarrow1.
\]
This establishes (3).

It remains to compare the conjectured expression with \(e^{-2}(n-1)!\). In the precise finite form relevant for each integer \(n\), put
\[
S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!(n-1)_k}.
\tag{28}
\]
Thus the proposed asymptotic term is
\[
T_n=e^{-2}\frac{n!}{n-2}(1+S_n)
\qquad(n>2).
\tag{29}
\]
The notation \(\sum_{k\geq1}\) in the conjectured expansion is represented here by the terms for which \((n-1)_k\neq0\), namely \(1\leq k<n\); terms with zero denominator are omitted. This is exactly the correction factor occurring in the stated conjecture.

We show that \(S_n\to0\). Separate its first term:
\[
S_n=-\frac1{n-1}+
\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!(n-1)_k}.
\tag{30}
\]
For \(2\leq k<n\), we have \(k!\geq2\), and
\[
(n-1)_k\geq(n-1)(n-2).
\tag{31}
\]
To see (31), split off the first two factors:
\[
(n-1)_k=(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)_{k-2};
\]
the final falling factorial is a positive integer because \(k<n\), and hence is at least \(1\). It follows that every summand in the second sum of (30) has absolute value at most
\[
\frac1{2(n-1)(n-2)}.
\tag{32}
\]
There are fewer than \(n\) such summands. Therefore, for \(n\geq3\),
\[
|S_n|
\leq \frac1{n-1}+ rac{n}{2(n-1)(n-2)}.
\tag{33}
\]
For \(n\geq4\), an elementary cross-multiplication gives
\[
\frac{n}{2(n-1)(n-2)}\leq\frac1{n-3}.
\tag{34}
\]
Indeed, all denominators are positive, and (34) is equivalent to
\[
n(n-3)\leq2(n-1)(n-2),
\]
whose right side minus left side is \(n^2-3n+4>0\). Thus
\[
|S_n|\leq\frac1{n-1}+\frac1{n-3}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{35}
\]
In particular, \(1+S_n\to1\) (and it is nonzero for all sufficiently large \(n\)). Also
\[
\frac{n}{n-2}=1+\frac2{n-2}\longrightarrow1.
\tag{36}
\]
Using \(n!=n(n-1)!\), we can divide (29) by the common benchmark from (3):
\[
\frac{T_n}{e^{-2}(n-1)!}
=
\frac{n}{n-2}(1+S_n).
\tag{37}
\]
Equations (35) and (36) show that the right side tends to \(1\). Hence
\[
T_n\sim e^{-2}(n-1)!.
\tag{38}
\]

Finally, both \(a(n)\) and \(T_n\) are asymptotic to the same eventually nonzero positive quantity \(e^{-2}(n-1)!\). Dividing the two corresponding ratios, or using transitivity of asymptotic equivalence, gives
\[
\frac{a(n)}{T_n}\longrightarrow1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
 a(n)\sim e^{-2}\frac{n!}{n-2}
 \left(1+\sum_{k\geq1}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!(n-1)_k}\right)
}
\qquad(n\to\infty),
\]
with the correction sum interpreted as in (28). This is the claimed asymptotic formula.
